title: Stokes' Law and Terminal Velocity
short_intro: Stokes' law describes the viscous drag force experienced by a small spherical body moving through a viscous fluid at low Reynolds numbers. It forms the theoretical basis for determining the coefficient of viscosity and calculating the terminal velocity of falling droplets.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of Stokes' force, dimensional formula of viscosity, dependence of viscous force on radius, velocity, and coefficient of viscosity, and simple terminal velocity problems.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Detailed dimensional derivation of Stokes' law, analysis of Reynolds number limitations, motion of bodies in rotating or accelerated frames involving viscous drag, and transient approach to terminal velocity.

prerequisites: Coefficient of viscosity and Newton's law of viscosity
Dimensional analysis and Buckingham Pi theorem

concept_notes.heading: Viscous Drag Force on Spheres
bullets: When a solid sphere of radius r moves with a uniform velocity v through an infinite, incompressible fluid of viscosity eta, it experiences a retarding force known as viscous drag.
The magnitude of this force is directly proportional to the radius of the sphere, its velocity, and the dynamic viscosity of the medium.
The direction of the Stokes' force is always opposite to the instantaneous relative velocity vector between the sphere and the fluid.

concept_notes.heading: Terminal Velocity
bullets: As a spherical body falls freely under gravity through a viscous fluid, its downward acceleration decreases due to the simultaneous increase in upward viscous drag and buoyant force.
When the magnitude of the gravitational force equals the sum of the upward buoyant force and the Stokes' drag force, the net force becomes zero.
At this stage, the body continues to fall with a constant maximum velocity known as the terminal velocity (v_t).

concept_notes.heading: Dependence and Scaling Factors
bullets: Terminal velocity varies directly as the square of the radius of the spherical body (v_t proportional to r<sup>2</sup>).
It is directly proportional to the density difference between the sphere (rho) and the fluid (sigma), and inversely proportional to the coefficient of viscosity (eta).
If the radius is doubled, the terminal velocity increases by a factor of four, assuming laminar flow conditions are maintained.

concept_notes.heading: Reynolds Number Validity Criterion
bullets: Stokes' law is strictly valid only when the flow pattern around the sphere is purely laminar and creeping, characterized by a very low Reynolds number (Re less than 0.1).
At higher Reynolds numbers, inertial forces dominate over viscous forces, leading to the formation of eddies and wake separation, causing deviations from Stokes' law.
Corrections (such as the Oseen correction) are applied when the Reynolds number approaches unity.

derivations.title: Dimensional Derivation of Stokes' Law
derivations.conditions: Assuming the viscous force F depends only on sphere radius r, velocity v, and fluid viscosity eta.
steps: Express the dependence in functional form: F = k * (r<sup>a</sup>) * (v<sup>b</sup>) * (eta<sup>c</sup>), where k is a dimensionless constant.
Substitute the dimensional formulas for each quantity: [F] = MLT<sup>-2</sup>, [r] = L, [v] = LT<sup>-1</sup>, and [eta] = ML<sup>-1</sup>T<sup>-1</sup>.
Equate the powers of fundamental dimensions M, L, and T on both sides: For M: c = 1; For T: -b - c = -2, yielding b = 1; For L: a + b - c = 1, yielding a = 1.
Substitute the exponents back into the initial expression to obtain F = k * eta * r * v.
derivations.result: F = 6 * pi * eta * r * v (where hydrodynamic integration yields k = 6 * pi)

derivations.title: Derivation of Terminal Velocity
derivations.conditions: A solid sphere falling freely under gravity in a viscous fluid under laminar flow conditions.
steps: Identify the forces acting on the falling sphere of volume V = (4/3)*pi*r<sup>3</sup> and density rho: Downward gravitational force W = V * rho * g.
Identify upward buoyant force B = V * sigma * g, where sigma is fluid density.
Identify upward viscous drag force F_s = 6 * pi * eta * r * v_t.
Apply equilibrium condition at terminal velocity: W = B + F_s, which gives V * (rho - sigma) * g = 6 * pi * eta * r * v_t.
Substitute V = (4/3)*pi*r<sup>3</sup> and solve for v_t.

formula_sheet.conditions: Laminar flow, spherical body, infinite medium, Re < 0.1

graphs_and_experiments.title: Velocity vs. Time Graph for a Falling Sphere
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A curve starting from origin (v = 0 at t = 0) showing an exponentially decreasing slope, asymptotically approaching a horizontal line representing terminal velocity v_t.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates that acceleration decreases continuously as viscous drag increases with velocity, eventually reaching zero when v = v_t.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in conceptual multiple-choice questions regarding the shape of the velocity-time curve in viscous media.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Stokes' Viscometer Experiment (Falling Sphere Method)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A tall glass jar filled with a transparent viscous liquid (like castor oil), marked with two reference rings separated by a fixed distance, with a small steel ball dropped inside.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: By measuring the time taken to fall between the reference marks, terminal velocity is computed, allowing the calculation of the liquid's viscosity.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested via questions on experimental precautions, such as ensuring the jar is wide enough to avoid wall effects.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Logarithmic Plot of Terminal Velocity vs. Radius Squared
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line passing through the origin on a v_t versus r<sup>2</sup> plot.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Confirms the linear relationship between terminal velocity and the square of the radius, validating Stokes' law experimentally.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used in PGT-level data interpretation and slope-based numerical problems.

solved_numericals.question: A small metal ball of radius 2 mm and density 8000 kg/m<sup>3</sup> falls through a liquid of density 1000 kg/m<sup>3</sup> and viscosity 0.8 Pa·s. Calculate its terminal velocity. (Take g = 10 m/s<sup>2</sup>)
solution_steps: Identify given values: r = 2 mm = 2 * 10<sup>-3</sup> m, rho = 8000 kg/m<sup>3</sup>, sigma = 1000 kg/m<sup>3</sup>, eta = 0.8 Pa·s, g = 10 m/s<sup>2</sup>.
Substitute values into the terminal velocity formula: v_t = \frac{2 * (2 * 10^{-3})^2 * (8000 - 1000) * 10}{9 * 0.8}.

solved_numericals.question: Two small identical spherical raindrops reach a terminal velocity of 2 m/s when falling separately through air. If coalesced into a single larger spherical drop, find the new terminal velocity.
solution_steps: Let the radius of each small drop be r and terminal velocity be v_1 = 2 m/s.
Volume conservation upon coalescence: \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = 2 * \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3, which gives R = 2^{1/3} * r.
Terminal velocity is proportional to the square of the radius: v_t \propto r^2.
Find ratio of new terminal velocity (v_2) to old (v_1): \frac{v_2}{v_1} = \left(\frac{R}{r}\right)^2 = (2^{1/3})^2 = 2^{2/3}.

solved_numericals.question: A spherical ball of mass m and radius r is projected vertically upwards with initial velocity v_0 in a viscous medium obeying Stokes' law. Find the time taken to reach the highest point.
solution_steps: Write down the equation of motion during upward motion: m*(dv/dt) = -mg - 6*pi*eta*r*v.
Rewrite as dv/dt = -g - (6*pi*eta*r / m)*v. Let k = 6*pi*eta*r / m. Then dv/dt = -(g + k*v).
Separate variables and integrate from t = 0 (v = v_0) to t = T (v = 0): \int_{v_0}^{0} \frac{dv}{g + kv} = - \int_{0}^{T} dt.
Substitute k = 6*pi*eta*r / m to get final expression for time T.

assumptions_and_limitations: The fluid must be unbounded (infinite in extent) so that wall effects do not alter the hydrodynamic drag.
The falling sphere must be perfectly rigid, smooth, and free from internal circulation or surface contamination.
The flow velocity must be sufficiently low to maintain laminar conditions without turbulence or wake separation (Re < 0.1).

common_misconceptions.wrong: Terminal velocity depends on the total distance the body falls through the fluid.
common_misconceptions.correct: Terminal velocity is independent of distance fallen once steady-state is achieved.
common_misconceptions.why: It is determined purely by the balance between gravitational, buoyant, and viscous forces.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Stokes' law applies to objects of any shape moving through a viscous fluid.
common_misconceptions.correct: Stokes' law is strictly formulated and mathematically derived only for spheres.
common_misconceptions.why: Non-spherical geometries require complex drag coefficients and shape correction factors (e.g., Faxen's corrections).

common_misconceptions.wrong: Viscous drag force increases continuously as the object falls indefinitely.
common_misconceptions.correct: Viscous drag force increases only until velocity reaches terminal velocity, after which it remains constant.
common_misconceptions.why: Once velocity becomes constant, the drag force stops increasing and remains equal to the effective weight.

quick_revision: Stokes' viscous drag is given by F = 6*pi*eta*r*v.
Terminal velocity varies directly as the square of the radius (v_t proportional to r<sup>2</sup>).
Stokes' law is valid only for creeping flow with Reynolds number less than 0.1.
The time constant for reaching terminal velocity is tau = (2*rho*r<sup>2</sup>) / (9*eta).
